A hardware wallet whose recovery phrase never touched the host has a different risk profile, but suspicious approvals and transactions still require review.
- Create clean keys and move assets carefully. Generate replacement keys on a clean hardware device or otherwise trusted environment. Verify the new receive address independently before moving assets. Prioritize according to value, exploitability, and current evidence; rushed signing on the infected host can worsen the incident.
- Revoke residual authority. Remove token approvals, disconnect sessions, rotate exchange API keys, invalidate developer tokens, and review smart-account delegates or session keys associated with the exposed wallet.
- Preserve and investigate. For an organizational device, contact the security team before wiping it. Preserve logs and forensic evidence, check other systems for the same initial-access path, and use current indicators from authoritative advisories as investigative leads.
- Rebuild trust. Reimage or replace the system under a documented process, patch it, reinstall only required software from verified sources, and restore data without restoring suspect executables or extensions.

### Do not make these incident mistakes

- Do not type the old recovery phrase into a “wallet checker,” cleanup site, or unsolicited support tool.
- Do not assume antivirus quarantine proves that credentials and sessions were not already stolen.
- Do not restore a compromised wallet by importing its old phrase into a new extension and call it rotated.
- Do not publish live forensic details, addresses, or evidence before considering attacker awareness and privacy.

### Limits and frequently asked questions

#### Does a hardware wallet make an infected PC safe?

No. It keeps keys off the computer when used correctly, but a compromised interface can still mislead the signer. Verify details on the hardware device.

#### Is changing the wallet password enough?

No. A local wallet password protects a particular encrypted store; it cannot make an already copied recovery phrase or private key secret again.

#### Should I wipe the device immediately?

For a personal device with no investigative need, rebuilding is often part of recovery. For a company or material-loss incident, coordinate evidence preservation first.

### Related Digibastion guides

Review seed phrase storage, compare hot and cold wallets, and rehearse the crypto hack response playbook before you need them.

## Exchange API Key Security for Trading Bots and Automation

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/articles/exchange-api-key-security-trading-bots
Updated: 2026-09-27

Treat every trading-bot credential as a bearer secret with a deliberately narrow blast radius. Give each workload its own key, remove withdrawal rights unless truly required, restrict origin where supported, keep secrets out of code, monitor use, and rehearse revocation.

Key takeaways:
- Use one narrowly scoped key per bot, environment, and account boundary; avoid shared all-powerful credentials.
- Apply exchange-supported permission and IP restrictions, and keep withdrawal capability separate from trading automation.
- Inventory, monitor, rotate, and revoke keys through a tested process that does not depend on the affected bot host.

Sources:
- Best Practices for Managing API Keys, Google Cloud: https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/api-keys-best-practices
- How to Create an API Key, Coinbase Help: https://help.coinbase.com/en/exchange/managing-my-account/how-to-create-an-api-key
- OKX API Guide: API Key Permissions and Security, OKX: https://www.okx.com/docs-v5/en/

### The direct answer

Secure trading automation by giving each bot and environment a separate, least-privileged API key; disabling withdrawal or transfer permissions unless the workflow truly requires them; restricting source IPs where the exchange supports it; storing secrets outside code and logs; monitoring every key; and maintaining a fast, tested revocation path from a device independent of the bot host.

### Why API keys need their own security design

An API key is a machine credential. Anyone who obtains the full credential set may be able to act with its assigned permissions until it is revoked or expires. Google Cloud's general API-key guidance recommends restrictions, deleting unnecessary keys, keeping keys out of client code and repositories, isolating keys by application and team member, rotating them, and monitoring use. The same lifecycle principles are useful for exchange automation, subject to each exchange's exact authentication model.

Exchange controls differ. Coinbase Exchange documentation separates view, trade, transfer, and manage permissions and requires an IP whitelist during key creation. OKX distinguishes read, trade, and withdraw permissions and recommends binding keys to IP addresses. Always verify the current controls in the official documentation and UI of the exact venue and account type you use.

### Threat model for a trading bot

#### Secret disclosure

Keys leak through repositories, build logs, screenshots, support tickets, shell history, environment dumps, backups, or a compromised developer or server.

#### Abuse within scope

A key without withdrawal access can still create harmful orders, reveal balances and strategy, or move value through trading if its permissions and risk controls allow it.

#### Pipeline compromise

A malicious dependency, CI runner, container image, or deployment operator may read the credential at build or runtime.

#### Control-plane failure

The team may detect abuse but be unable to identify, revoke, or replace the correct key without stopping unrelated systems.

### A secure architecture checklist

- One workload, one key. Separate production from development, strategy A from strategy B, and bot service from human access. Unique keys make revocation and attribution practical.
- Start with no withdrawal capability. Grant only the documented read or trade operations the bot needs. If funds must move, use a separate, tightly governed workflow and key rather than adding withdrawal rights to the trading bot.
- Use account boundaries. Where the venue supports portfolios or subaccounts, isolate bot balances and permissions so one automation failure cannot reach every asset.
- Restrict where credentials can be used. Bind the key to stable egress IP addresses when supported. Treat allowlisting as defense in depth: a compromised allowed server can still use the key.
- Keep secrets out of source and artifacts. Inject credentials at runtime from a managed secret store. Prevent them from entering browser code, mobile apps, repositories, container images, test fixtures, crash reports, or logs.
- Limit who and what can retrieve the secret. The bot runtime should receive only its own key. Developers, CI jobs, observability tools, and support staff should not gain production-secret access by default.
- Add trading guardrails outside the credential. Apply venue and bot controls for maximum order size, instruments, leverage, daily loss, price deviation, and kill conditions where supported. Permission scope alone does not prevent destructive but authorized trades.
- Monitor by key identity. Alert on unusual source IPs, permission changes, authentication failures, new instruments, order-rate changes, balance changes, and activity outside expected operating windows.

### Key lifecycle and rotation

- Inventory: record owner, bot, venue, account boundary, permissions, IP restrictions, creation date, last use, rotation deadline, and emergency contact—never the secret value in the inventory.
- Issue: create keys through an approved account, verify scope and restrictions before adding funds, and use a second reviewer for privileged capabilities.
- Deploy: deliver the secret through the secret-management path, run a minimal-permission test, and confirm that disallowed operations fail.
- Rotate: create a replacement, deploy it, confirm expected operation, revoke the old key, and verify that the old credential can no longer authenticate.
- Retire: delete keys when bots, vendors, developers, or environments are decommissioned. An unused credential is avoidable attack surface.

Rotation frequency should reflect venue capability, exposure, and operational risk. A calendar is useful, but rotate immediately after suspected disclosure, unauthorized use, access changes, or compromise of a system that could read the credential.

### Response steps for a suspected key leak

- Stop the blast radius. Disable the bot and revoke the affected key from a trusted administrative device. If key identity is uncertain, revoke the candidate set rather than preserving uptime at the expense of account safety.
- Use venue controls. Cancel unauthorized or risky open orders, reduce exposure, and contact the exchange through a verified support or institutional channel if activity or access cannot be controlled.
- Preserve evidence. Retain exchange audit history, key metadata, source IPs, order events, application logs, deployment history, and secret-access logs without copying secrets into the incident ticket.
- Determine the exposure path. Search repositories and history, CI logs, artifacts, host telemetry, dependency changes, support systems, and staff access. Rotating without closing the leak can expose the replacement.
- Review the account, not just the key. Inspect permissions, allowlists, account security, linked applications, balances, transfers, orders, and other credentials. Rotate related secrets when the same host or store could access them.
- Restore narrowly. Issue a new key with the minimum scope and a new secret-delivery path, validate restrictions, then resume at limited capacity while monitoring closely.

### Limits and frequently asked questions

#### Is disabling withdrawals enough?

No. It is an important reduction in impact, but trading permission can still create losses or manipulate positions. Add balance isolation and trading guardrails.

#### Does an IP allowlist make a leaked key harmless?

No. It blocks use from other sources, but an attacker controlling an allowed server or network path may still succeed. Keep all other controls.

#### Should secrets be encrypted in a config file?

Encryption can help only if decryption authority is better protected. Prefer a managed secret system with workload identity, access logs, and narrowly scoped retrieval over shipping ciphertext and its effective unlock path together.

### Related Digibastion guides

Extend the design with centralized exchange security practices, the password and secret-storage guide, and the software supply-chain defense guide.

# Checklists

## Crypto Wallet Security Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/wallet

Secure your cryptocurrency assets

- Use hardware wallet: Store significant amounts in a hardware wallet
- Backup seed phrase: Securely store your seed phrase offline
- Use multiple wallets: Separate hot and cold storage wallets
- Enable transaction signing: Require password/biometrics for transactions
- Regular security audit: Periodically review wallet security settings
- Test recovery process: Practice wallet recovery with small amounts
- Use watch-only wallets: Monitor holdings without exposing private keys

## OpSec Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/opsec

Protect your digital footprint and operations

- Map your on-chain footprint: Understand what information is publicly visible on blockchain
- Use address separation: Use different addresses for different transaction types
- Consider privacy-enhancing technologies: Use ZK protocols and privacy-focused solutions
- Implement transaction verification: Verify all transactions before execution
- Use multi-signature for high-value transactions: Require multiple approvals for treasury operations
- Deploy transaction simulation tools: Verify transaction outcomes before execution
- Establish clear wallet security procedures: Document air-gapped setups and seed phrase backups
- Implement separation of duties: Different roles for transaction approval stages
- Define tiered wallet architecture: Set thresholds for different security requirements
- Establish remote team security protocols: Device security and secure home network guidelines
- Use end-to-end encrypted communications: Secure channels for sensitive discussions
- Implement hardware security keys: Use Yubikeys or Passkeys as primary 2FA
- Conduct thorough security audits: Multiple independent audits for critical contracts
- Implement upgradability patterns: Use proxy patterns with governance mechanisms
- Use formal verification: Mathematical proofs for critical contract functions
- Deploy circuit breakers and timelocks: Time-delayed administration and value limits
- Develop community security guidelines: Security policies for open-source contributors
- Establish code review processes: Multi-level review and bug bounty programs
- Balance transparency with security: Clear guidelines on information sharing
- Pre-travel device preparation: Minimize sensitive data and enable encryption
- Secure 2FA for travel: Backup codes and disable SMS-based authentication
- Hardware wallet travel security: Never travel with written seed phrases
- Research border crossing laws: Understand local encryption and tech regulations
- Secure network usage while traveling: Use cellular data or personal hotspots over public WiFi
- Avoid public USB charging: Use your own charger or USB data blocker
- Delay social media location posts: Post location updates 1-2 days after leaving
- Post-travel security review: Change passwords and scan devices after returning
- Implement layered protection: Multiple overlapping security controls
- Apply minimal access scopes: Grant only necessary permissions
- Maintain system isolation: Segment systems into isolated security zones
- Enable continuous visibility: Active monitoring and security testing
- Use burner devices for high-risk travel: Minimal data devices that can be wiped post-trip
- Enable Lockdown Mode: Maximum security for high-risk situations
- Increase multisig requirements while traveling: Geographically split key custody during travel

## DeFi Security Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/defi

Secure your DeFi interactions and investments

- Hardware Wallet Integration: Secure high-value DeFi positions
- Independent Security Audits: Verify protocol security
- Smart Contract Addresses Verification: Verify contract transparency

## Authentication Security Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/authentication

Secure your accounts with strong authentication methods

- Use a Strong Password: Generate long and complex passwords.
- Don't Reuse Passwords: Keep passwords unique across accounts.
- Use a Secure Password Manager: Store and generate passwords securely.
- Avoid Sharing Passwords: Keep your credentials to yourself.
- Enable Two-Factor Authentication: Secure logins with an extra verification step.
- Keep Backup Codes Safe: Secure your 2FA recovery codes separately.
- Adopt Wallet-Based Authentication: Leverage cryptographic wallet signatures for login.
- Sign Up for Breach Alerts: Monitor your emails for potential data breaches.
- Shield Your Password/PIN: Conceal your credentials during entry.
- Update Critical Passwords Periodically: Refresh important passwords annually.
- Don't Save Passwords in Browsers: Avoid browser-based password storage.
- Avoid Logging In on Untrusted Devices: Limit access on public or shared devices.
- Avoid Password Hints: Do not use easily guessable hints.
- Never Answer Security Questions Truthfully: Provide fictitious answers to security questions.
- Avoid 4-Digit PINs: Use longer passcodes for better security.
- Avoid Using SMS for 2FA: Prefer app-based or hardware 2FA methods.
- Separate OTP Generation from Password Manager: Use a dedicated app for generating OTPs.
- Avoid Face Unlock: Reconsider using facial recognition for authentication.
- Watch Out for Keyloggers: Inspect your devices for keylogging threats.
- Consider a Hardware Security Token: Add a physical layer to your 2FA strategy.
- Consider an Offline Password Manager: Manage your passwords offline for extra security.
- Use KeePassXC with Passkeys Support: Store passkeys in your local password manager.
- Consider Unique Usernames: Use distinct identifiers for each service.

## OS Hardening Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/os

Strengthen your operating system security

- Keep Your System Up-to-Date: Install security patches and updates promptly.
- Encrypt Your Device: Enable full disk encryption.
- Isolate Crypto Wallet & Node Operations: Run crypto apps in dedicated environments.
- Backup Important Data: Maintain secure, encrypted backups.
- Be Cautious with USB Devices: Avoid plugging in untrusted USB devices.
- Activate Screen-Lock When Idle: Automatically lock your computer when not in use.
- Enable firewall: Configure and enable system firewall
- Review Your Installed Apps: Minimize installed applications.
- Manage Application Permissions: Control app access to sensitive data.
- Disallow Usage Data to Cloud: Limit automatic data syncing.
- Avoid Quick Unlock Methods: Use strong passwords over biometrics or short PINs.
- Power Off Instead of Standby: Shut down your device when not in use.
- Use antivirus software: Install and maintain updated antivirus protection
- Enable Secure Boot: Prevent unauthorized bootloader modifications.
- Use a Local Account Only: Avoid linking your PC to online accounts.
- Use Non-Admin Accounts for Daily Tasks: Avoid running as a root or admin user.
- Block Webcam and Microphone: Prevent unauthorized access to your camera and mic.
- Use a Privacy Screen Filter: Protect against shoulder surfing.
- Physically Secure Your Device: Prevent unauthorized physical access.
- Avoid Charging from Untrusted Sources: Use a power bank or wall charger instead of your PC.
- Randomize Your Hardware Address on Wi-Fi: Change your MAC address to reduce tracking.
- Disable Unnecessary Sharing Services: Turn off network sharing features you don't use.
- Protect Against Software Keyloggers: Use tools to encrypt keystrokes.
- Check for Hardware Keyloggers: Inspect your keyboard connections.
- Prevent Keystroke Injection Attacks: Lock your device when not in use.
- Avoid Commercial 'Free' Antivirus Software: Rely on built-in or reputable security tools.
- Guest account control: Disable or restrict guest accounts
- Periodically Check for Rootkits: Scan for deep system infections.
- Set a BIOS/UEFI Boot Password: Add an extra layer before OS boot-up.
- Use a Security-Focused Operating System: Consider hardened OS distributions.
- Utilize Virtual Machines: Isolate risky tasks in VMs.
- Compartmentalize Your Work: Separate programs and data sources.
- Disable Unwanted Windows Features: Turn off unnecessary background services.
- Secure SSH Access: Harden your remote login configuration.
- Close Unused Open Ports: Limit services listening on your network.
- Implement Mandatory Access Control: Restrict privileges and limit process capabilities.
- Deploy Canary Tokens: Set up alerts for unauthorized access.
- Use Qubes OS for Maximum Isolation: Run activities in separate virtual machines.
- Use Portmaster Application Firewall: Monitor and control application network access.
- Consider Coreboot Firmware: Replace proprietary BIOS with open-source firmware.
- Implement VM Compartmentalization Strategy: Isolate different activities in dedicated VMs.

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/email

Secure your email communications for Web2 and Web3

- Explore Decentralized Email Solutions: Consider blockchain-based alternatives for email.
- Use Multiple Email Addresses: Separate critical communications from casual mail.
- Secure Your Email Account: Protect your inbox with strong credentials.
- Keep Your Primary Email Private: Avoid public exposure of your main email address.
- Disable Remote Content Loading: Prevent automatic downloads in emails.
- Switch to a Secure Email Provider: Opt for privacy-focused email services.
- Don't Transmit Sensitive Data via Email: Avoid sending confidential information unencrypted.
- Avoid Third-Party App Access: Limit external app permissions to your email.
- Prefer Plaintext Emails: Opt for plaintext for better privacy.
- Leverage Email Aliasing: Use unique aliases for different services.
- Employ Email Subaddressing: Use '+' tagging to manage incoming mail.
- Utilize a USB Smart Key: Store your encryption keys offline.
- Adopt a Custom Domain: Use your own domain for email addresses.
- Backup Your Emails Locally: Sync your emails using a client for redundancy.
- Be Cautious with Email Signatures: Avoid including excessive personal data.
- Use Auto-Replies Sparingly: Limit automatic responses to protect information.
- Select Secure Mail Protocols: Avoid outdated and insecure email protocols.
- Avoid Self-Hosting Unless Expert: Self-hosting email is risky without advanced skills.
- Always Use TLS Ports: Enforce encrypted connections for email.
- Ensure DNS Redundancy: Maintain multiple MX records for reliability.
- Mitigate DDoS and Brute Force Attacks: Limit connections on your mail server.
- Maintain an IP Blacklist: Regularly update blacklists for your mail server.

## Browsing Security Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/browsing

Secure your online browsing experience

- Use a Web3-Enabled Browser or dApp Isolation: Secure decentralized interactions with specialized browsers.
- Block Ads: Use an ad blocker to reduce tracking.
- Use a Privacy-Respecting Browser: Choose browsers that protect your data.
- Use a Private Search Engine: Switch to non-tracking search engines.
- Remove Unnecessary Browser Extensions: Limit installed addons to reduce risk.
- Keep Your Browser Updated: Apply updates to patch vulnerabilities.
- Use HTTPS Websites: Ensure sites use encrypted connections.
- Enable DNS-over-HTTPS: Encrypt your DNS queries.
- Use Browser Containers: Isolate different browsing sessions.
- Use Incognito/Private Mode: Browse privately on shared devices.
- Monitor Your Browser Fingerprint: Understand how unique your setup is.
- Manage Your Cookies: Regularly clear cookies to reduce tracking.
- Block Third-Party Cookies: Prevent external sites from tracking you.
- Block Third-Party Trackers: Use tools to stop background tracking.
- Beware of Malicious Redirects: Verify URLs before following redirects.
- Avoid Browser Sign-in: Don't sync personal data with your browser.
- Disable Prediction Services: Turn off search and URL predictions.
- Avoid Google Translate Extensions: Limit data collection from translation tools.
- Disable Browser Notifications: Stop unsolicited push alerts.
- Disable Automatic Downloads: Prevent drive-by download attacks.
- Restrict Sensor Access: Control websites' access to device sensors.
- Disable Location Services: Stop sites from tracking your physical location.
- Block Camera/Microphone Access: Prevent unauthorized use of your devices.
- Disable Browser Password Saving: Avoid storing credentials in the browser.
- Turn Off Browser Autofill: Prevent accidental exposure of sensitive data.
- Guard Against CSS Exfil Attacks: Mitigate data extraction via CSS.
- Deactivate ActiveX Controls: Disable ActiveX to reduce risk.
- Disable WebRTC: Prevent IP leaks through peer-to-peer connections.
- Spoof Canvas Fingerprint: Obfuscate your browser's canvas signature.
- Spoof User Agent: Change your browser's user agent periodically.
- Disable Do Not Track: Stop sending DNT signals.
- Mitigate HSTS Tracking: Reduce risks associated with HSTS super-cookies.
- Disable Automatic Browser Connections: Prevent your browser from calling home.
- Enable First-Party Isolation: Scope browser data to each website.
- Strip Tracking Parameters: Remove tracking info from URLs.
- Secure First Launch: Configure privacy settings before browsing.
- Use the Tor Browser: Browse anonymously using Tor.
- Disable JavaScript: Reduce potential attack surfaces.
- Use a VPN for Browsing: Encrypt your internet traffic.
- Use Privacy-Focused DNS: Opt for DNS providers that respect your privacy.
- Use Custom DNS Firewall Lists: Block malicious domains at the DNS level.
- Add Crypto Phishing Filter Lists to uBlock Origin: Block Web3 phishing and scam sites.
- Enable Built-in Tracking Parameter Stripping: Use browsers that automatically remove URL trackers.
- Use LibRedirect for Privacy-Friendly Frontends: Redirect to privacy-respecting alternatives.
- Use NoScript for JavaScript Control: Granularly control which sites can run scripts.
- Use DNSCrypt or Oblivious DoH: Encrypt DNS with advanced privacy protocols.
- Use a Privacy-Focused VPN: Choose VPNs with strong privacy guarantees.
- Harden Browser Fingerprinting Protection: Enable advanced anti-fingerprinting in Brave.
- Use Browser Profiles for Isolation: Create separate browser profiles for different activities.

## Mobile Security Checklist

URL: https://www.digibastion.com/category/mobile

Essential security measures for mobile devices in the Web3 era

- Use a Secure Mobile dApp Wallet & Browser: Access decentralized apps safely on mobile.
- Encrypt Your Device: Enable full-disk encryption to secure your data.
- Turn Off Unused Connectivity Features: Disable Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, etc., when not in use.
- Keep App Count to a Minimum: Remove unused applications from your device.
- Manage App Permissions: Review and limit what data apps can access.
- Install Apps Only from Official Sources: Use trusted app stores for downloads.
- Use strong PIN/password: Set up a strong device password with minimum 6 characters
- Enable biometric authentication: Set up fingerprint or face recognition for device access
- Install security updates: Keep your device updated with latest security patches
- Set Up a Mobile Carrier PIN: Secure your SIM with a carrier PIN.
- Be Cautious with Public Charging: Avoid 'juice jacking' risks at public charging stations.
- Opt-out of Caller ID Listings: Keep your phone number more private.
- Use Offline Maps: Leverage offline navigation to limit location data leakage.
- Opt-out of Personalized Ads: Reduce targeted advertising and data collection.
- Enable Data Erasure After Multiple Failed Logins: Automatically wipe your device after too many failed attempts.
- Monitor App Trackers: Identify and review trackers in your apps.
- Use a Mobile Firewall: Monitor and block unwanted app traffic.
- Reduce Background Activity: Limit apps running in the background.
- Sandbox Mobile Apps: Isolate apps to protect your data.
- Avoid Custom Virtual Keyboards: Stick with the device's stock keyboard.
- Restart Your Device Regularly: Clear caches and temporary data with periodic reboots.
- Avoid SMS for Sensitive Communications: Use encrypted messaging instead of SMS.
- Keep Your Number Private: Utilize virtual numbers to protect your identity.
- Watch Out for Stalkerware: Detect and remove spyware installed by others.
- Favor the Browser Over Dedicated Apps: Use secure browsers to access services.
- Security app installation: Install mobile security/antivirus app
- Route Mobile Traffic via Tor: Use Tor to anonymize your mobile network traffic.
- Consider a Custom ROM (Android): Switch to a privacy-focused OS for better control.
- Enable Per-Connection MAC Address Randomization: Randomize your MAC address for each network.
- Use Offline User Profiles: Create profiles that never connect to the internet.
- Use Obtainium for Verified APKs: Fetch APKs directly from source repositories.
- Use Aurora Store as Play Store Alternative: Access Play Store apps anonymously.
- Use Privacy-Focused Offline Maps: Navigate without sharing location data.
- Use Anonymous SMS Services: Receive SMS without revealing your real number.
- Use Privacy-Focused Mobile Data: Get mobile connectivity without identity linkage.
